transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-06
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~53 minutes
Attendees: Alex Reed (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Noah Kim (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (DataHarbor Eng Manager), Samira Patel (DataHarbor SRE), Michael Torres (Product), Eve Wong (Security)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping focused on benchmark planning and integrating DataHarbor's customer scripts into Redwood's benchmark harness. Discussed workload sizing, streaming vs non-streaming semantics, success criteria (p95 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens), and timelines for a 3-week POC. Next steps: share harness, customer provides scripts, schedule run-with-us session.

Topics:
- Workload characterization (latency targets, concurrency, input lengths)
- Harness integration details (python scripts, container, auth)
- Streaming vs non-streaming benchmark tradeoffs
- Security and deployment constraints (VPC, KMS, audit logs)
- Success criteria and acceptance tests

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Reed: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick round of intros?
[00:06] Jordan Lee: Jordan here, eng manager for inference at DataHarbor.
[00:09] Samira Patel: Samira, SRE, I run our load infra and metrics.
[00:12] Michael Torres: Michael, product manager covering recommendations.
[00:14] Eve Wong: Eve from security, a couple questions later.
[00:17] Alex Reed: Great. Alex from Redwood, AE, and Priya and Noah from our solutions team. Today we want to scope the POC — specifically the benchmark plan, how we plug your scripts into our harness, and define success criteria.

[02:05] Priya Shah: To start, can you walk through the three representative workloads you mentioned in the doc? We want to make sure we size concurrency and sequencing correctly.
[02:14] Jordan Lee: Yeah, sure. We have 1) short chat-like prompts for customer support replies, avg length ~35 tokens in prompt and we expect ~80 tokens response; 2) a document summarization flow — long inputs, avg prompt 2k tokens, output 200–400 tokens; 3) a re-ranking/embedding style batch throughput job — we send 5k items per minute, embedding size 1536.

[04:01] Priya Shah: Nice, that helps. For the chat workload are you doing streaming responses in prod?
[04:07] Jordan Lee: Yes, chat is streamed to the UI for low perceived latency. Summaries are non-streaming, batch. The re-rank is a high-throughput non-streaming pipeline.

[05:20] Samira Patel: For the streaming path, we're concerned about tail latency and also token-level cost. Our internal SLO is p95 < 250ms for single-turn chat (on our current infra).

[05:35] Alex Reed: Ok, that's helpful. For a POC our usual success metrics are: p50/p95 latency for 1–8 concurrent users, tokens/sec throughput for batch flows, end-to-end cost per 1M tokens, and correctness/regression on quality tests. We'll align to your p95 target but we need to instrument at both request-level and token-level.

[07:10] Priya Shah: On the harness side we support two modes: 1) harness-driven load where we run your scripts inside our runner (we mount your script + inputs into a container and run repeatable scenarios), or 2) we run a lightweight shim on your side that calls our API and streams metrics back. Which is easier for you?

[07:35] Jordan Lee: We prefer to keep our secrets on our side, so a shim might be better. But we'd rather not re-engineer everything — how heavy is the shim?

[07:50] Priya Shah: Typically the shim is a small Python process ~200 lines, uses your existing client library, emits JSON traces, and can run a replay with fixed timestamps or a concurrency ramp. Auth can be via short-lived API key or mTLS.

[08:22] Noah Kim: And if you prefer we can also run inside your network in a private runner — that's what we do for some Private deployments, but that needs a quick kube job or Docker runner.

[09:00] Michael Torres: If we run the shim we need to measure streaming vs non-streaming differences. For example, streaming has lower time to first token but higher total CPU on the server due to context switching. Can your harness measure token-level timings?

[09:20] Priya Shah: Yes, we instrument token-level timestamps when streaming is enabled; we'll capture time-to-first-token, inter-token jitter, and end-of-stream. For non-streaming we capture total request latency and server-side token generation time. There's sometimes some noise in transcription — sorry, I mean instrumentation — when middle proxies buffer.

[11:00] Samira Patel: For sizing we need to decide on concurrency matrix. Our baseline: 100 concurrent chat users (typical peak), 8–16 concurrent summarization jobs, and the re-rank embedding pipeline runs as a separate worker with steady 5k items/min.

[11:23] Alex Reed: Good. For the POC we'll propose a test matrix: chat — 1, 5, 20, 100 conc; summaries — single-threaded and 8 conc; embeddings — 1 worker, 5k/min steady and a 10k/min stress. Does that sound realistic?

[11:44] Jordan Lee: Yes, that aligns. Also we want to run both cold-start and warm runs — because caching/KV cache really helps after warm-up.

[12:02] Priya Shah: We'll include warmup phases. We'll also send an instrumentation snippet you can drop into your shim that toggles KV cache warming and logs cache hit rates. Note — sometimes our auto-prefix cache is called KV cash in the internal notes so watch for that, small typo in our docs.

[13:15] Eve Wong: A few security constraints from my side: we need audit logs for all tokenized requests, KMS integration for keys, and proof that no customer data persists in shared hosts. If you run any harness inside our VPC, we need the runner to respect Egress rules.

[13:42] Alex Reed: Understood. For Private or Dedicated modes we can do a runner inside your VPC and use your KMS/HSM. For hosted runs we'll use short-lived keys and we can scrub logs; we'll provide SOC2 docs and an architecture diagram.

[14:10] Eve Wong: Also our legal/compliance team will want a data flow diagram and retention policy.

[14:18] Alex Reed: We'll send our security pack after this call — I'll add that to next steps.

[15:30] Priya Shah: Back to harness integration — what's the expected format of your scripts today? Are they plain Python, or do you have a microservice that already does the orchestration?

[15:40] Jordan Lee: Mostly Python scripts that call our internal client (wrapped around OpenTelemetry), sometimes a small FastAPI microservice. We can adapt. We'll aim to provide 3 sample scripts: chat_stream.py, summarizer_batch.py, embed_worker.py.

[17:05] Noah Kim: Great. For the chat_stream.py we'll want to run it in streaming mode and capture token timings. We'll also want to run identical prompts non-streaming to compare end-to-end latency and cost.

[17:20] Jordan Lee: Good call. We'll include a set of 200 prompts that mirror production percents (60% short, 30% medium, 10% long).

[18:30] Samira Patel: How long is the POC window you're proposing? We need to coordinate infra and calendar.

[18:36] Alex Reed: Usually 2–3 weeks: week 1 — harness setup and smoke tests; week 2 — full runs and tuning; week 3 — analysis and regression checks. If we find issues early we can compress, but three weeks gives us proper runs.

[19:05] Michael Torres: That works. For success criteria we want: p95 chat latency < 250ms (streaming to UI), summarization p95 < 2.5s, embeddings throughput >= 5k/min with cost below our current baseline (we'll share current $/1M tokens). Also no functional regression on 10 evaluation prompts.

[19:28] Priya Shah: We'll produce an evaluation dashboard with those KPIs and include traces, flamegraphs for token generation hot spots, and a cost breakout. We'll also report model variants and quantization used.

[20:10] Jordan Lee: On models, we plan to test 1) small quantized variant for cost, 2) medium accuracy variant, 3) a high-accuracy baseline (we may compare to Anthropic and OpenAI for quality). Would you be able to swap models during runs?

[20:28] Priya Shah: Yes — our harness supports rolling tests across model variants and automatic fallback in case of OOMs. Just note that quantized variants may change latency profile; we'll capture that.

[21:15] Samira Patel: A nuisance question — where do you run the benchmark from? Is there any network egress that would skew latency?

[21:24] Noah Kim: We can run from our hosted region (us-west1) or spin a runner inside your VPC to eliminate internet hops. For p95 latency targets we recommend an in-region runner.

[22:02] Jordan Lee: We'll prefer an in-VPC runner for the definitive runs. For initial smoke we can use hosted.

[22:20] Alex Reed: Perfect. Now about measurement fidelity: we recommend you capture both client-side and server-side metrics. Client-side captures network and UI time; server-side gives exact token generation time. Combined we can explain differences.

[24:00] Priya Shah: One practical note: streaming test results can be noisier because of buffering in proxies — we've seen CDNs or internal proxies coalesce tokens. We'll add jitter testing and a proxy-check test.

[25:12] Michael Torres: For embeddings pipeline, we need to measure tail latency per item and overall throughput. Also cost normalization per 1M tokens is less meaningful here; convert to $/1M embedding calls or $/1M tokens equivalently.

[26:00] Priya Shah: We'll prepare cost normalizers for embeddings and text. We'll also include recommendations: batch size tuning, quantization profile, and concurrency knobs.

[27:50] Jordan Lee: If we find that streaming latency is fine but cost is high, we'd likely consider a hybrid: first token streamed, then non-streamed aggregation for larger responses. Can the harness simulate that?

[28:03] Priya Shah: Yes we can script hybrid flows — stream first N tokens, then do a non-stream finish. We'll include that as an optional test case.

[29:30] Eve Wong: Regarding compliance: if the runner is agent inside our VPC, what is the data retention by Redwood?

[29:40] Alex Reed: For private runners we can set retention to 0 or to whatever policy you need; hosted runs keep short-term traces for debugging but we can redact payloads and scrub logs. We'll follow up with an explicit retention table.

[31:10] Samira Patel: A corner case — summarization of long docs hits memory OOM on some quantized kernels. If that occurs, will Redwood automatically fallback to a compatible variant?

[31:25] Priya Shah: We have automatic fallback rules: if OOM or kernel fail, route to a larger instance or de-quantized model variant, and we capture that in logs. For POC we'll enable the fallback but also record every fallback as an event.

[33:45] Jordan Lee: One thing we want is reproducibility — each run should have a run-id, commit id for the harness, and model version. Can you enforce that in output artifacts?

[33:55] Noah Kim: Absolutely — every run artifact includes run_id, harness git sha, model name + sha, and the exact config used. We'll put that into the dashboard download.

[35:00] Michael Torres: On dashboards, can we get token-level cost broken down by model, quantization, and batch size?

[35:06] Priya Shah: Yes — cost breakout is one of our standard panels. We'll also show per-model CPU/GPU utilization and per-request memory.

[36:40] Alex Reed: Let's recap timelines: Alex to share harness repo and README by 2026-10-08, Priya to draft streaming vs non-streaming test plan by 2026-10-09, Jordan to upload scripts by 2026-10-12, schedule run-with-us the week of 2026-10-19 for the big runs. Anything to add?

[37:05] Jordan Lee: We'll confirm calendar by EOD. Also we'll attach current cost baseline numbers and the 10 eval prompts.

[37:18] Eve Wong: Security follow-ups will come via email. We may request a short architecture call if needed.

[37:25] Alex Reed: Sounds good. Any risks we should call out?

[37:30] Samira Patel: Biggest risk is env parity — if we run hosted and then you run in-VPC, results may differ due to network and instance types. We'll call out those differences and recommend the in-VPC run for final acceptance.

[38:05] Priya Shah: Also model parity — quantization can change quality. We'll include a small eval suite to measure delta against your quality baseline.

[38:35] Jordan Lee: Good. One more operational ask: can you provide a short runbook for the shim so our infra folks can review?

[38:45] Alex Reed: Yes, we'll include a runbook + minimal Dockerfile.

[39:20] Priya Shah: Ok, technical note: for streaming we'll instrument time-to-first-byte and also per-token gap. If you see >150ms gaps between tokens that likely indicates batching at the serving tier.

[40:10] Michael Torres: We care about perceived latency on mobile — so TTFB matters more than total.

[40:20] Jordan Lee: We'll add a mobile app trace to the evaluation in a later phase. For POC keep mobile as a proxy.

[41:12] Alex Reed: Any final questions?

[41:20] Eve Wong: None from me right now, will send over the security list.

[41:25] Samira Patel: No more from infra.

[41:30] Jordan Lee: All good. Thanks.

[41:35] Alex Reed: Awesome — recap of next steps in chat. We'll follow up with harness link and schedule invite. Thanks everyone.

[52:50] Call ends.
